newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: OPINION- S.Africa's 1996/97 budget - By E.Osborn.
newsitem.headline: OPINION- S.Africa's 1996/97 budget - By E.Osborn.

text.p: By Edward Osborn, consultant to Edey, Rogers (Pty) Ltd
By good fortune rather than good management the outcome for the 1996/97 budget deficit turned out to be almost precisely the same as originally budgeted.

Higher expenditures were fortuitously matched by higher-than-expected revenues so that the net deficit turned out to be 28.9 billion rand, or 5.1 percent of GDP, as originally planned, according to recently released Exchequer returns.

It is of interest, though that if capital receipts were taken out of the deficit calculations, as is now the budgetary accounting practice, the deficit would be 5.5 percent of GDP. Comparably, the budgeted four percent for 1997/98 is on this basis.
Gross revenues and expenditure were markedly different.
Revenue received into the Exchequer amounted to 148.66 billion rand, as compared with the budget projection of 144.86 billion rand, the difference being due to higher inland revenue figures.

But the detailed revenue figures, which are only available through to February, show, suprisingly, much higher than expected revenues from sources other than income taxes and VAT, the major revenue items.
Certainly the promised windfall receipts flowing from improved collections and the collection of amounts in arrear on these two items seem to have been achieved.

However, in the eleven months receipts from so-called departmental activities were already 1.5 billion rand in excess of full-year estimates, interest and dividends 450 million rand greater and revenue from trade securities 140 million rand greater.

The reason for the sharp increase in departmental activities will only be identified in next year's budget, one can only speculate and a possibility is sales of capital equipment and sales of state-owned land, both of which are a from of capital revenue.

Although subsequently larger than in the original budget, departmental issues from the exchequer were well within the much increased authorisations to spend approved in the February Additional Estimates budget.
Indeed the full estimates for the year, excluding the double-counting of the RDP expenditures which have bugged the estimates in the last few years, ended up as 189.6 billion rand.
With the total requisitions for the year amounting to 177.6 billion, the implication would be that there will be a roll-over of authorisations of 12 billion rand.
These could spook fiscal management in 1997/98, but the Minister has given assurances of the strictest surveillance being maintained over them.

They do provide an ultimate safety value for over-restricted departments in the 1997/98 fiscal year. Many of the votes fall into this category because of the Minister's Procrustean drive to achieve the 4 percent deficit.

Interest payments of the Ministry of Finance vote amounted to 33.5 billion rand, or 5.9 percent of GDP, almost precisely as estimated. In addition there were forex costs on foreign debt redeemed of nearly 1 billion rand included in the requisitions - this being the accounting practice as foreign loans to be redeemed are given at the original rand values.

In effect then ordinary revenues of 146.8 billion rand exceeded non-debt related expenditures, that is on goods, services and transfers, of 143.1 billion rand. Such a primary surplus budget is somewhat deflationary as more revenue is drawn from the economy than disbursed in the form of expenditure.

Together with capital receipts, it is, however, the principal means of moving towards the ultimate goal of a 3 percent deficit. And, indeed, the ultimate GEAR objective of a 3 percent deficit is effectively a commitment to deflationary budgets.

Such was again the case in this year's budget where a debt servicing bill amounting to 6.4 percent of GDP had to be offset by a primary surplus in order to arrive at the overall 4 percent deficit. The debt servicing ration to GDP ought to be reducing and it is a matter of concern that it has actually jumped from 5.9 percent to 6.4 percent, which entails the need for a growing primary surplus.

The total funding requirement in the year amounted to 48.1 billion rand. This was needed to meet the deficit as well as domestic loan redemptions of 16.4 billion rand, foreign loan redemptions at original value of 1.9 billion, honouring guarantees and late requisitions in respect of past years amounting to only 495 million rands, etc.

Surrenders of 4.8 billion rand, however, effectively reduced this to 43,3 billion rand, against which 39.5 billion rand was raided in the domestic and foreign loan markets, A further net increase in short term borrowings of 2.4 billion rand assisted in the financing.
But it was still necessary to draw on cash balances to the tune of 1.4 billion rand to complete the financing.
Total public debt figures at the end of March 1997 are not available as yet, although the Ministry of Finance estimated it at 55.5 percent of GDP in the budget Review.
As far as local registered stock is concerned this grew by 27.4 billion rand in the year to a total value of 275.6 billion rand despite the large volume of stock redeemed.

Zero-interest stock increased by 3.5 billion rand to 14.8 billion rand, which helped to reduce the average coupon rate of interest on total local registered stock from 11.57 percent to 11.46 percent. The average coupon rate on interest bearing stock, however, was reduced slightly from 12.125 percent o 12.108 percent.

All in all the Ministry of Finance must be well satisfied with the outcome for the 1996/97 fiscal year, although there has emerged the incubus of the relentlessly growing interest bill and the engulfing roll-overs.
(The opinions expressed in this article represent those of the author only. They should not be seen to represent the views of Reuters.)
